classification.difficultyReason: Requires comparison of an absolute-value graph with a rational graph, two poles, exact intersections and an isolated equality point.

content.prompt: By using appropriate graphs, solve the inequality $$\frac{1}{x^2-1}\ge |x|-1.$$

inlines.text: Compare the rational graph with the V-shaped graph; exclude both poles and retain the isolated equality at

answer.worked:
Sketch $y=\dfrac{1}{x^2-1}$ and $y=|x|-1$. The rational graph is undefined at $x=\pm1$.

For intersections, put $t=|x|$, where $t\ge0$ and $t\ne1$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{1}{t^2-1}&=t-1\\1&=(t-1)^2(t+1)\\t(t^2-t-1)&=0\\t&=0\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.\end{align*}$$
The other quadratic root is negative, so it is inadmissible for $t=|x|$. Thus the graphs intersect at $x=0$ and $x=\pm\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$.

The rational graph is on or above the V-shaped graph between each pole and the adjacent outer intersection, and also at the isolated point $x=0$. Hence
$$-\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\le x<-1\quad\text{or}\quad x=0\quad\text{or}\quad1<x\le\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.$$

spec.description: Authored common-axis comparison of the rational and absolute-value functions, with both poles and all three intersections.
spec.mathematics: Intersections x=0 and x=±(1+sqrt(5))/2; vertical asymptotes x=±1; isolated equality at (0,-1).
